cells.tense: The practice is here, being kept, and you are the one at it now.
cells.act: stand in the gap it leaves without rebuilding yet
cells.ask: When a stretch of sessions goes quiet before you've decided to stop, don't fill the silence with a new plan. Stay in the empty days, and choose nothing until something chooses itself.
cells.core:
You know how to do a thing in your own corner, in the repetitions nobody watches. That is the practice held here, and today it is in your hands. It runs steady without gripping: on good days the hour passes in attention and then it's done, and being alone with it feels like company rather than a wall.

What's easy to miss is that some part of the practice is already falling away — a routine gone stale, a shape you've outgrown — and the falling is not the loss. When that happens, the pull is to rebuild at once with something new. Instead, stand in the gap a day or two before you decide anything. What comes down that needed to come down clears space the next thing will use.

Nothing in you has to be forced today. Sit down and keep it easy.
cells.sheetLine: Let the gap stay open a day before you fill it.
cells.verb: keeping the fire lit across the days when it barely shows
cells.place: the practice corner where the work is done alone, day after day

cells.tense: The practice is being braced against a next session that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Say to yourself that one routine is finished, then set it down this week and go days without replacing it. Choose it before you feel ready.
cells.core:
You get up and it starts: run the routine, check the form, do it again. Any day that lapses reads as evidence against you. The doing has turned into defending — a refinement that exists to make the next refinement necessary, the correction that proves you caught it in time. Nobody watching can tell, but you can. The tell is that stopping is what scares you.

On the other side of this, practicing is quieter. The refinement serves the work rather than your standing in it, and being alone is chosen rather than required. The way back runs through completion: one routine you've carried past its use is already finished. Declare it done to yourself, set it down deliberately, and go days without replacing it. Grip isn't what keeps the practice good; the practice is. Testing that is the point.

cells.tense: Something about the old practice still has you, though it sits behind you now.
cells.act: trade one thing for one thing, and keep no score
cells.ask: Do ten minutes of one practice that once went bad, then ten minutes of something you enjoy, and let the evening be even. No ledger.
cells.core:
There's a way of training that got set down somewhere back along the way, and it didn't stop being yours just because you stopped. You can picture what it would ask: the same time tomorrow, and the day after. Wanting a routine again sits a little like approaching a door that closed once.

So don't aim for the whole shape. Pick one practice and trade it evenly — ten minutes of it, then ten minutes of something you'd choose anyway. The exchange is the point: the practice gets its share and you get yours, and neither side is carrying the other. What's owed here is small, and it's paid in full the moment both sides are met.

A little practice and a little of your own, matched, is what the old door needs. Not the full load.
cells.sheetLine: Trade it even. Practice gets its hour, you get yours.
cells.verb: keeping the fire lit across the days when it barely shows

cells.tense: The practice is being kept by you right now, and the keeping isn't being counted.
cells.act: let the path show itself instead of forcing clarity
cells.ask: Next time a skill comes out of your hands and you can't say how it got there, explain nothing. Do the next small thing with it and notice what happens.
cells.core:
There's a thing you've grown good at in private — a way you hold the pen, a way you play, a form you hit — and as far as you tell it, it simply showed up. You haven't called it practice in a long time, if ever. The ability is real. What's gone quiet is the accounting: what looks like a gift usually has years under it that nobody's been keeping.

That doesn't make the skill less. It means your improvement has been arriving as something that happens rather than as a hand you can see doing it. Rather than explain where it came from, let the next step show itself — do the small thing the skill is asking for, and skip the story about how you got here. Keep your hands on the work, not on the account of it.
cells.sheetLine: The skill is real, but the practicing has gone unnamed.
cells.verb: keeping the fire lit across the days when it barely shows
cells.place: the practice corner where the work is done alone, day after day
